# Exploring the Relationship Between Teachers' AI Attitudes, AI Self- Efficacy, and AI Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge

Mustafa Erol[1](mailto:)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1675-7070)\| Merve Canbeldek Erol[2](#european-journal-of-education)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3100-2220)\| Ahmet Erol[2](#european-journal-of-education)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7538-952X)\| Feride Gök Çolak[3](#european-journal-of-education)

1Department of Primary Education Program, Yıldız Technical University, İstanbul, Türkiye \| 2Department of Preschool Education Program, Pamukkale University, Denizli, Türkiye \| 3Department of Preschool Education Program, Yıldız Technical University, İstanbul, Türkiye

**Correspondence:** Mustafa Erol ([merol@yildiz.edu.tr)](mailto:merol@yildiz.edu.tr) **Received:** 18 March 2025 \| **Revised:** 23 October 2025 \| **Accepted:** 24 October 2025

**Funding:** The authors received no specific funding for this work. **Keywords:** artificial intelligence attitude \| artificial intelligence self- efficacy \| artificial intelligence- technological pedagogical content knowledge

## ABSTRACT This study examines the relationships between teachers' attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI), AI self- efficacy, and AI technological pedagogical content knowledge (AI- TPACK). The participants comprised 524 teachers working in preschool and primary schools. Data were collected using AI attitude, AI self- efficacy, and AI- TPACK scales. Pearson correlation analysis and structural equation modelling (SEM) were employed for data analysis. The findings indicate that teachers' AI self- efficacy is significantly and positively associated with AI attitudes and AI- TPACK. Furthermore, teachers' positive attitudes toward AI significantly influenced their AI- TPACK and AI self- efficacy. In contrast, negative attitudes toward AI were negatively correlated with AI self- efficacy but did not show a significant relationship with AI- TPACK. Additionally, AI- TPACK played a mediating role in the relationship between attitudes toward AI and AI self- efficacy. These findings contribute to the growing body of research on teachers' attitudes toward AI, AI self- efficacy, and AI- TPACK.

**1.1 \| AI in Education: Opportunities and Challenges**

In early childhood education, AI applications have been found to support cognitive development, enhance motor skills, fa- cilitate language acquisition, and strengthen socio- emotional learning (Chen  [2024;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Kazu and Kuvvetli  2023, 2025; Su and Zhong 2022). AI- powered tools can improve children's collab- oration, communication, and problem- solving skills while fos- tering active participation in learning processes (Aravantinos et al. [2024;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Çelik [2023;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Fikri and Rhalma 2024). By promoting computational thinking, AI enhances students' self- efficacy, knowledge, skills, and positive attitudes, as well as their learn- ing experiences (Massaty et  al.  2024; Yang et  al.  2024; Zhao et  al.  2024). Additionally, AI offers engaging and interactive methods for deep learning and achieving educational goals (Kazu and Kuvvetli 2023; Yi et al. 2024).

However, ethical, security, and privacy concerns have also emerged regarding AI applications (Neugnot- Cerioli and Laurenty  2024). Safeguarding children's privacy and well- being requires careful attention to how AI systems manage personal data, ensure identity protection, and implement ro- bust digital security measures (Edeni et al. [2024)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). Lemaignan et al. (2021) warn that the misuse of AI may lead to identity theft, financial risks, and the creation of fraudulent profiles. In addition, exposure to inappropriate content, geolocation tracking, and biometric vulnerabilities pose further risks to children's safety (Liu and Ding  2025). The potential of AI- driven systems to influence children's cognition or manipu- late their thinking also demands critical consideration (Bakir et al. [2024)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). Effective and safe integration of AI into education requires teachers to cultivate informed and positive attitudes toward AI, develop the competence to align AI tools with ped- agogical aims, and possess the necessary content knowledge to apply them meaningfully (Flink and Cooper- Larsen 2020; Ning et al. 2024).

**1.2 \| Attitudes Toward AI**

An attitude can be defined as a person's cognitive, emotional, and behavioural evaluation of an object, idea, or process (Petty et al. 2003). In this context, teachers' attitudes and views on new technologies significantly impact how they are incorporated into the classroom (Falebita and Kok 2025; Nazaretsky et al. 2022; Obenza et al. 2024). According to Ayanwale et al. ([2022)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7), atti- tudes toward AI refer to people's opinions and assessments, whether favourable or unfavourable, of AI tools and their 

function in learning contexts. According to the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), people's atti- tudes and adoption behaviours are directly influenced by their perception of technology, including perceived effort, social im- pact, and institutional support (Dwivedi et al. [2011)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). According to a study, educators with positive attitudes toward technology are more likely to include AI tools in their lesson plans (Adelana et al. [2024;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Obenza et al. 2024).

While some educators are open to using technology in their lessons, others could be resistant and favor more conventional teaching resources and techniques. Such hesitancy frequently results from doubts about the usefulness of AI tools in educa- tion, perceived difficulties in utilising AI, and restricted access to professional development opportunities (Hébert et al. 2021). Many educators admit to lacking theoretical and practical ex- pertise in the educational applications of AI, despite acknowl- edging the technology's potential (Chounta et al. [2022)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). A study on the adoption of AI in education identifies several significant obstacles, including unfavorable perceptions of AI, a lack of technological proficiency among educators and learners, moral dilemmas, and difficulties in customising AI tools to meet ed- ucational requirements (Crompton et al. [2024)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). However, pro- moting favorable perceptions of AI is not enough to ensure its successful integration into the classroom. The successful in- tegration of AI technologies into teaching practices relies on teachers' adoption and effective use of these tools, which is closely linked to their self- efficacy in AI.

**1.3 \| AI Self- Efficacy**

A person's confidence in their ability to complete a task is known as self- efficacy (Bandura [1977)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). According to McCoy (2010), self- efficacy refers to an individual's ability to master a skill and is strongly associated with their confidence in performing the tasks necessary for success. In the educational setting, a teacher's con- fidence in using AI tools effectively in their professional practice is known as AI self- efficacy (Yang  2025). Teachers with high levels of AI self- efficacy are more likely to learn about AI, solve problems, and integrate it into their lessons to achieve learning objectives (Sun et  al.  2023). The increasing integration of AI in education requires teachers to expand their knowledge and skills in this area continuously (Wang et al. 2023). Enhancing AI self- efficacy strengthens pedagogical and technological com- petencies, enabling educators to design more effective learning environments. Research suggests that teachers with positive at- titudes toward educational technology often demonstrate greater confidence in its use, and this relationship is mutually reinforcing (Yang 2025). Moreover, technology self- efficacy, which is influ- enced by elements including early exposure to digital tools, fre- quency of usage, and availability of technology, is directly linked to AI self- efficacy (Koć- Januchta et al. 2022). Pan (2020) empha- sises that individuals' willingness to adopt new technologies is powerfully shaped by their level of technological self- efficacy.

AI tools are more likely to be used in teaching by educa- tors with greater levels of digital literacy (Liwanag and Galicia  2023). Prior experience in online learning environ- ments enhances individuals' proficiency in utilising AI- based tools, as these tools facilitate self- directed learning 

processes (Masry- Herzallah and Watted 2024). AI systems can strengthen self- efficacy while optimising learning experiences (Flink and Cooper- Larsen  2020; Loftus and Madden  2020). However, teachers' successful application of AI technologies goes beyond AI self- efficacy and needs to be considered in the context of the larger Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) paradigm. The TPACK model empha- sises the interplay of pedagogical, technological, and topic knowledge. It offers a structured approach to understanding how teachers may effectively incorporate AI- based resources into their lesson plans. In this context, AI- TPACK refers to educators' ability to integrate AI tools with pedagogical and disciplinary knowledge to ensure their effective application in educational settings (Bergdahl and Sjöberg [2025)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7).

**1.4 \| AI- TPACK**

AI- TPACK equips teachers with the competencies required to manage technology- enhanced instructional processes by inte- grating pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) with technological knowledge (TK). PCK remains a key foundation, encompassing teachers' expertise in representing content accessibly, addressing misconceptions, and adapting instruction to learners' develop- mental levels (Shing et al. 2018). When integrating AI tools, teach- ers must draw upon their PCK to evaluate whether such tools genuinely support conceptual understanding and to adjust their pedagogy accordingly (Bautista et al. [2024;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Su 2024). However, while PCK provides this pedagogical foundation, recent evidence suggests that AI- specific TPACK exerts a greater influence on teachers' capacity to integrate AI into learning processes (Ning et  al.  2022, 2024; Bergdahl and Sjöberg  [2025)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). Teachers with strong AI- TPACK are thus better equipped to translate their pos- itive attitudes toward AI into meaningful, curriculum- aligned instructional practices (Bergdahl and Sjöberg [2025)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7).

Effective AI integration in education requires that teachers not only possess the technological infrastructure but also com- prehend the pedagogical implications of AI and strategically embed it into their instructional practices (Çelik [2023;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Seufert et al. 2021). By doing so, they can enhance student motivation and engagement through the purposeful use of AI- based tools (Wang et  al.  2021). In this regard, embedding AI within the TPACK framework is essential for preparing teachers to operate effectively in technology- driven learning environments (Karataş and Ataç 2025). The incorporation of AI into the TPACK frame- work highlights the dynamic interplay between pedagogy and technology, promoting individualised learning opportunities and necessitating a reevaluation of traditional teaching prac- tices (Karataş and Yüce 2024; Casal- Otero et al. [2023)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). Through this framework, teachers develop the capacity to design cre- ative, student- centered learning experiences by combining their understanding of AI technologies with pedagogical strategies and subject- matter expertise (Sun et al. 2023).

**1.5 \| Current Study: AI- TPACK as a Mediating Variable**

Rethinking curricula, teaching strategies, and assessment de- signs within the context of AI- supported techniques is crucial 

to maximising the potential of AI in education (Eltabakh and Ahmed Ismail 2019; Su and Zhong 2022). Wang (2024) exam- ined the evolving roles of instructors, the transformation of educational environments, and the integration of artificial intel- ligence into learning processes. Developing AI literacy is crucial for teachers to effectively integrate this technology into their in- structional practices (Zhao et al. 2022). However, while previous studies have highlighted key components of AI's pedagogical applications, a comprehensive understanding of how teachers adopt AI, perceive their AI self- efficacy, and relate these per- ceptions to AI- TPACK remains limited (Choi et  al.  [2023;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Du and Gao  [2022)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). Further research is needed on teachers' atti- tudes toward AI and their self- efficacy in using AI. Most cur- rent studies on AI integration in education focus on secondary school teachers or specific subject areas (Bautista et al. [2024)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). However, the pedagogical strategies employed by preschool and primary school teachers in relation to AI, as well as their atti- tudes and self- efficacy in using AI, remain underexplored (Zhao et al. 2022).

Teachers' capacity to successfully incorporate AI into their classrooms may be hindered by their concerns about the po- tential negative impacts of AI on young students (Stolpe and Hallström  2024). While teachers generally exhibit positive attitudes toward AI, their self- efficacy in using AI is closely linked to their ability to integrate it within the AI- TPACK framework (Gentile et al. 2023). Expanding teachers' under- standing of AI's educational applications is crucial for ensur- ing positive attitudes translate into practical, safe classroom practices. AI- TPACK may mediate the relationship between teachers' attitudes toward AI and their AI self- efficacy (Ning et al. 2024). A positive attitude toward AI can encourage teach- ers to explore ways to incorporate it into their instruction. However, to achieve effective AI integration and self- efficacy, teachers must understand how AI aligns with pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) (Bergdahl and Sjöberg [2025)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). This process enhances teachers' TPACK development, helping them grasp how AI tools can be effectively utilised in educa- tional settings.

Synthesising these insights, a conceptual framework can be pro- posed: _Attitude_ → (influences) _Knowledge_ (AI- TPACK) → (influ- ences) _Self- Efficacy_ (Bergdahl and Sjöberg [2025)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7).

**1.6 \| Research Aim and Research Questions**

The present study examines the relationships among teachers' at- titudes toward AI, AI self- efficacy, and AI- TPACK. Specifically, it examines the mediating role of AI- TPACK in the relationship between teachers' attitudes toward AI and their self- efficacy in AI. The study aims to determine how AI- TPACK shapes the con- nection between AI attitudes and AI self- efficacy, as illustrated in the proposed model (Figure 1). The following research ques- tions guide the study:

- Is there a relationship between teachers' AI self- efficacy, AI attitudes, and AI- TPACK?
- Does the relationship between teachers' AI attitudes and AI self- efficacy get mediated by AI- TPACK?

**2 \| Method**

**2.1 \| Participants**

In a metropolitan area in northwest Türkiye, a total of 524 teach- ers from 21 primary schools and eight preschools participated in this study. The purposive sampling approach was employed to ensure the selection of individuals who could provide the most relevant data for the study's objectives (Patton 1990). The par- ticipating teachers provided their voluntary consent after being informed about the purpose and procedures of the study, and it was clearly stated that participation was entirely voluntary. There were 63.4% female participants (_n_ = 332) and 36.6% male partici- pants (_n_ = 192). Regarding educational background, 67.9% held a bachelor's degree (_n_ = 356), while 32.1% had completed graduate- level education (_n_= 168). Regarding teaching specialisation, 61.8% were primary school teachers (_n_ = 324), whereas 38.2% were preschool teachers (_n_ = 200). The teachers' ages ranged from 26 to 57 years, and their teaching experience varied between 5 and 33 years.

**2.2 \| Data Collection Tools**

**2.2.1 \| The General Attitudes Toward AI Scale (GAAIS)**

Schepman and Rodway  (2023) developed the GAAIS to measure individuals' overall sentiments toward AI. Kaya et al. (2022) adapted the scale into Turkish. It consists of 20 items, divided into two subscales: 8 for negative attitudes (negative AAI) and 12 for positive attitudes (positive AAI). A five- point Likert scale (where 1 is ‘strongly disagree’ and 5 is ‘strongly agree’) is used to score the items. After reversing the negatively worded items, total scores on the scale range from 20 to 100, with higher scores indicating more positive attitudes toward AI. The internal consistency reliability of the scale was reported as _α_ = 0.88 for the Positive GAAIS and _α_ = 0.83 for the Negative GAAIS (Schepman and Rodway  2023). An example item from the Positive subscale is: “Artificial Intelligence can provide new economic opportunities for this country.” An example item from the Negative subscale is: “Organisations use Artificial Intelligence unethically.” Four experts translated the scale into Turkish for the Turkish ad- aptation, and linguistic and AI education experts reviewed the translated items. The Turkish version of the GAAIS was validated and closely resembles the original English version (Schepman and Rodway 2023; Kaya et al. 2022). In the present study, Cronbach's alpha was calculated as _α_ = 0.90 for both the 

Positive and Negative AAI subscales, indicating high internal consistency.

**2.2.2** \| **AI Self- Efficacy Scale—Short Form**

Montag et al. (2023) developed the AI self- efficacy scale—short form to assess teachers' self- efficacy in using AI technologies. Türk et al. (2025) adapted the scale into Turkish. It comprises five items under a single- factor structure and is rated on a seven- point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree). The possible total scores on the scale range from 7 to 35, with higher scores indicating greater self- efficacy in using AI tools. The original scale's internal consistency reliability was reported as Cronbach's alpha = 0.77 (Montag et al. 2023). The present study calculated Cronbach's alpha as 0.87, indicating high internal consistency. Example items from the scale in- clude: “I can easily use AI tools,” and “Using AI tools is very complicated for me.”

**2.2.3** \| **AI- TPACK Scale**

The AI- TPACK scale, developed by Ning et  al.  (2024), assesses teachers' knowledge and competencies in integrating AI tech- nologies into education. Canbazoğlu Bilici et al. ([2024)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) adapted the scale into Turkish. The AI- TPACK scale comprises seven subdimensions and 39 items, measured on a 5- point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree). CFA results indi- cated that the Turkish version retained the original factor struc- ture. The total possible score ranges from 39 to 195, with higher scores indicating more excellent AI- TPACK proficiency. The in- ternal consistency reliability of the original scale was reported as Cronbach's alpha = 0.98. For the subdimensions, reliability values were: Content Knowledge (CK): _α_ = 0.87, Pedagogical Knowledge (PK): _α_= 0.89, AI- Technological Knowledge (AI- TK): _α_ = 0.95, Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK): _α_ = 0.93, AI- Technological Content Knowledge (AI- TCK): _α_ = 0.97, AI- Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI- TPK): _α_ = 0.97, AI- TPACK: _α_ = 0.95 (Canbazoğlu Bilici et al. [2024)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). In the present study, Cronbach's alpha values were calculated as follows: CK: _α_ = 0.88, PK: _α_ = 0.89, AI- TK: _α_ = 0.95, PCK: _α_ = 0.89, AI- TCK: _α_ = 0.95, AI- TPK: _α_ = 0.96, AI- TPACK (Overall): _α_ = 0.94. Sample items:

- CK: “I fully understand the historical development of the concepts and principles related to the subject I teach.”
- PK: “I am knowledgeable about effective classroom man- agement and organisation.”
- AI- TK: “I am proficient in accessing AI technologies needed for teaching.”
- PCK: “I am aware of students' common misconceptions in the learning process.”
- AI- TCK: “I can select appropriate AI technologies based on the subject I teach.”
- AI- TPK: “I have the competency to use AI technologies to enhance my pedagogical perspective.”
- AI- TPACK: “I am proficient in selecting instructional meth- ods and AI technologies appropriate for the course content.”

**2.3 \| Data Collection Process and Ethical Considerations**

Throughout the entire research process, this study closely ad- hered to ethical guidelines. Teachers were given comprehensive information about the study's goals, parameters, and methods from the outset. Written consent forms were used to secure in- formed consent, guaranteeing voluntary involvement. Teachers were assured that they might leave at any time without suffering any repercussions. They were also informed that their identities would remain anonymous throughout the study and that their data would be kept confidential in accordance with ethical pri- vacy guidelines. Special care was taken to protect participant confidentiality when presenting the results, and no personally identifiable information was shared. Data collection was sched- uled at appropriate times to minimise disruptions to their profes- sional responsibilities, ensuring that the process did not interfere with their daily workload. No coercion was applied to encourage participation, and teachers completed the surveys individually. On average, completing the scales took 15 to 20 min. All collected data were digitally recorded with the assistance of a research as- sistant. The integrity of the data was strengthened by a secondary verification procedure that was carried out to guarantee accu- racy and dependability.

**2.4 \| Data Analysis**

**2.4.1 \| Preliminary Analysis**

To initiate the data analysis process, we presented descriptive statistics. To assess the internal consistency of the teacher's re- sponses to the questions, we calculated the Cronbach's alpha coefficient. We computed the Pearson correlation coefficient to ascertain the strength and direction of the relationships between the variables. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) was then em- ployed to examine the factor structure of the measurement in- struments. To evaluate the validity of the measurement model, we computed many goodness- of- fit indices. Tucker- Lewis Index (TLI) and Comparative Fit Index (CFI) values greater than 90 were deemed appropriate. Additionally, it was expected that the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) and Standardised Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) values would be below 0.08 (Byrne [2010)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7).

**2.4.2** \| **Main Analysis**

Data analysis was conducted using JAMOVI (2.3.38). Key de- scriptive statistics, including mean, standard deviation, frequen- cies, and correlation values, were initially computed. Skewness and kurtosis indicators were analysed to evaluate the normal- ity assumption, considering acceptable values within the range of −1.96 to +1.96 (George and Mallery 2010). Additionally, the mean and standard deviation for all variables were calculated. To analyse the direct and indirect effects within the model, we employed bias- corrected bootstrapping procedures with 2000 bootstrap samples (Hayes  2017). Direct effects were repre- sented using single- headed arrows. Next, we applied Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) to examine the mediating role of AI- TPACK in the relationship between AI attitudes and AI 

self- efficacy. We implemented a GLM mediation model to test whether AI- TPACK mediated the connection between AI atti- tudes and AI self- efficacy. Additionally, we analysed the direct, indirect, and total effects of AI attitudes and AI- TPACK on AI self- efficacy to better understand their influence on teachers' confidence in integrating AI into educational settings. For pa- rameter estimation, we applied the maximum likelihood esti- mation method, which is recognised as an optimal approach. SEM was performed using the jAMM module, and confidence intervals were determined using the Delta method, an extension of the Central Limit Theorem (Deng et al. [2018)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7).

**2.5 \| Reliability and Validity of the Measurement Model**

A thorough assessment of the measuring model's psychomet- ric qualities was conducted. For every scale, Cronbach's alpha and Composite Reliability (CR) values exceeded the 80% cut- off, indicating strong internal consistency. Furthermore, the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) values for each construct were more significant, at 0.50, indicating the scales' convergent validity. Each concept met the requirements and aligned with the recommendations made by Hair (2019) in the discriminant validity analysis conducted using the Fornell- Larcker crite- rion  (1981). These results imply that the measurement model is valid and dependable for evaluating the intended constructs. The SRMR values were lower relative to the model fit indices 

0.08 on every measure, suggesting a well- fitting model (Hu and Bentler 1998). Additionally, all scales had NFI values more sig- nificant than 0.90, indicating a satisfactory model fit (Bentler and Bonett [1980)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). Detailed analysis revealed that the AI attitude scale, with its two- factor structure, demonstrated acceptable fit indices (_χ_2/df = 2.25, RMSEA = 0.07 \[0.06, 0.08\], SRMR = 0.06, CFI = 0.92, TLI = 0.91). Similarly, the AI- TPACK scale, which comprises seven dimensions, exhibited acceptable fit indices (_χ_2/ df = 2.12, RMSEA = 0.07 \[0.07, 0.08\], SRMR = 0.05, CFI = 0.93, TLI = 0.92). Meanwhile, with its unidimensional structure, the AI self- efficacy scale demonstrated excellent fit (_χ_2/ df = 1.38, RMSEA = 0.04 \[0.001, 0.01\], SRMR = 0.02, CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.99). The values in parentheses represent the 90% confi- dence interval of RMSEA.

**3 \| Findings**

**3.1 \| Correlation Analysis Results**

The correlation coefficients for the teacher variables, including AI- TPACK, AI attitude, and AI self- efficacy, are presented in Table 1. The findings reveal a moderately significant positive relationship between AI self- efficacy and AI- TPACK (_r_ = 0.50, _p_ \< 0.001). Similarly, a positive and significant correlation was found between a positive AAI and AI- TPACK (_r_ = 0.45, _p_ \< 0.001). Additionally, AI self- efficacy and positive AAI showed a low but significant correlation (_r_ = 0.18, _p_ \< 0.01). Conversely, negative AAI and AI self- efficacy were shown to be significantly correlated negatively (r = −0.20, _p_ \< 0.01). Negative AAI and AI- TPACK, however, did not significantly correlate (_p_ \> 0.05). Additionally, Table 1's skewness and kur- tosis values show that the distributions of the variables lie 

within the normalcy range, or between −1.96 and 1.96, indi- cating that the normality requirements were satisfied.

**3.2 \| Mediating Effect Model**

Table  2 presents the direct, indirect, and total effects of pos- itive AAI, negative AAI, and AI- TPACK on AI self- efficacy. Examining the indirect effects, it was found that AI- TPACK mediates the effect of positive AAI on AI self- efficacy, and this indirect effect is statistically significant (_β_ = 0.23, _p_ \< 0.001, 95% CI \[0.098, 0.206\]). This suggests that AI- TPACK has a strong mediating effect on the relationship between positive AAI and AI self- efficacy. In contrast, the indirect effect of negative AAI was insignificant (_β_ = −0.01, _p_ = 0.745, 95% CI \[−0.057, 0.040\]). Regarding direct effects, positive AAI did not significantly af- fect AI self- efficacy (_β_ = −0.05, _p_ = 0.387, 95% CI \[−0.117, 0.045\]). However, negative AAI had a significant direct effect (_β_ = −0.19, _p_ = 0.001, 95% CI \[−0.239, −0.061\]). The analysis results indicate

This finding suggests that AI attitudes directly and indirectly contribute to AI self- efficacy. Furthermore, a post hoc power analysis confirmed that the sta- tistical power was strong (statistical power = 0.89, _α_ = 0.05) and that the sample size was sufficient. Therefore, a small sample size cannot be blamed for the non- significant results. The GLM model and _β_ coefficients are presented in Figure 2.

**4 \| Discussion**

This study investigates the relationships between teachers' at- titudes toward AI, their AI self- efficacy, and their AI- TPACK. The findings reveal that teachers' AI self- efficacy is positively correlated with favorable attitudes toward AI and negatively correlated with unfavorable attitudes toward AI. This implies that instructors' positive attitudes regarding AI rise in tandem with their level of AI self- efficacy. In contrast, lower levels of AI self- efficacy may be linked to more negative attitudes toward AI. These findings align with previous research, which suggests that attitudes play a crucial role in influencing an individual's will- ingness to adopt technology (Ayanwale et al. [2022;](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7) Mutambara and Chibisa  2022). Thus, positive AI attitudes can enhance teachers' ability to integrate AI tools effectively into learning environments (Oran 2023; Simuţ et al. 2024). Conversely, neg- ative attitudes toward AI may reduce teachers' confidence in AI applications. Previous research has also demonstrated that while lower AI self- efficacy might contribute to more unfavor- able impressions of AI, higher AI self- efficacy can result in more 

teachers' AI self- efficacy and AI- TPACK. Teachers' understand- ing and proficiency in incorporating AI into pedagogical pro- cesses improve as they get more comfortable with the technology. According to this research, teachers' ability to successfully

incorporate AI into their teaching methods depends on their level of self- efficacy, which is a question of personal confidence. According to prior studies, self- efficacy is crucial in technolog- ical integration processes (Kent and Giles  2017; Liwanag and Galicia 2023). Individuals' attitudes and behaviours regarding the adoption and effective utilisation of technology are strongly shaped by their level of technological self- efficacy (Alanzi et al. [2023)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). A positive correlation was found between technolog- ical self- efficacy and the adoption of online learning, suggesting that individuals with higher self- efficacy are more inclined to engage with and adapt to digital learning environments (Masry- Herzallah and Watted 2024). Teachers' readiness to incorporate AI into classrooms is influenced by TPACK and self- efficacy (Sun et al. 2023). Additionally, teachers' capacity to incorporate AI technology into pedagogical approaches is significantly en- hanced by AI- TPACK (Ning et al. 2024). The results of this study support the interrelated roles of pedagogical knowledge and self- efficacy in AI integration, aligning with the existing body of previous literature.

This study also found that teachers' attitudes regarding AI fa- vourably correlate with their AI- TPACK. In contrast, no signif- icant relationship was found between AI- TPACK and negative attitudes toward AI. As teachers' AI- TPACK levels increase, their positive attitudes toward AI also improve. However, neg- ative attitudes do not appear to directly influence AI- TPACK levels. As teachers' pedagogical and technological knowledge increases, they may develop a more positive outlook on AI. At the same time, their negative attitudes do not necessarily im- pact their AI- TPACK levels. Similarly, existing literature empha- sises that attitudes toward AI influence the adoption of AI tools (Falebita and Kok  2025). According to research by Ingersoll and Strong (2011), instructors' attitudes and interest in a sub- ject have a significant impact on their teaching. Research in- dicates that teachers who are optimistic about technology also tend to view TPACK elements more positively (Raygan and Moradkhani 2022; Tondeur et al. 2020; Voithofer et al. 2019). Furthermore, a teacher's positive attitudes are more likely to result in successful implementation if they acquire a strong AI- TPACK framework (Ning et al. 2024). Teachers' perceptions of AI tools can significantly influence the shaping of instructional practices and student learning outcomes (Yue et al. 2024). The fact that negative AI attitudes and AI- TPACK did not signifi- cantly correlate implies that negative attitudes may have only a minimal impact on knowledge levels.

AI- TPACK emerged as a crucial mediating variable that strengthens the relationship between teachers' attitudes to- ward AI and their self- efficacy in AI. While positive attitudes 

alone did not directly predict higher self- efficacy, negative at- titudes significantly reduced teachers' confidence in using AI. However, when mediated through AI- TPACK, favourable atti-

et al. 2024). A favourable outlook on AI can also motivate ed- ucators to investigate ways to incorporate this technology into their teaching methods. However, teachers must comprehend how AI aligns with pedagogical and topic knowledge for effec- tive integration and the development of self- efficacy (Bergdahl and Sjöberg [2025)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). Prior studies have shown a strong correla- tion between instructors' attitudes toward AI- based instruc- tion, pedagogical understanding, and content knowledge (Yue et al. 2024). Understanding teachers' levels of AI self- efficacy is important to ensure that AI technologies are integrated into education safely, effectively, and in alignment with pedagogical principles (Chiu et al. [2025)](#acknowledgements-https-doi-org-10-1186-s4059-4--023--00418---7). These results underscore the im- portance of equipping educators with pedagogical knowledge related to AI, enabling the integration of relevant and secure AI in the classroom.

**4.1 \| Limitations and Future Directions**

This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. Although the use of SEM provided an appropriate analytical framework for testing the proposed relationships, the study's cross- sectional design limits the ability to draw causal inferences regarding the directionality among variables. Future research employing longitudinal or experimental designs would offer stronger evidence for causal mechanisms underlying the asso- ciations between AI attitudes, AI- TPACK, and AI self- efficacy. The generalisability of the findings is limited, as the sample con- sisted exclusively of teachers working in Türkiye. Broader cross- cultural comparisons would allow researchers to examine how teachers' perceptions, self- efficacy, and pedagogical understand- ing of AI vary across different educational and cultural contexts. Such comparative analyses could deepen understanding of the contextual and cultural dynamics influencing AI integration in education. Considering the decisive mediating role of AI- TPACK, the development of targeted professional development programs aimed at enhancing teachers' AI- TPACK competence is strongly recommended. Strengthening these competencies could simultaneously improve teachers' self- efficacy, foster more positive attitudes toward AI, and ultimately support the effective and ethical adoption of AI in classrooms.

**5 \| Conclusion**

This study investigates the relationships between teachers' atti- tudes toward AI, their AI self- efficacy, and their AI- TPACK. The results indicate that positive attitudes alone are insufficient for effective AI adoption in education. Teachers must also possess the pedagogical, technological, and content integration skills necessary to apply AI tools purposefully and ethically. Those
